description:
An Eared Dove (Zenaida auriculata), photographed at Plaza ConstituciÃ³n in Montevideo, Uruguay. [Local name: Torcaza Común.] This documents one of my encounters with this close relative of the Mourning Dove (Zenaida macroura).   It differs from the Mourning Dove in that it has a dark eyeline, a dark (usually bluish-black) auricular spot, a bluer/grayer cast to its flight feathers, fewer dark spots on its tertiaries, and shorter and darker tail feathers.  This is a common bird in Uruguay and can be found anywhere that water is avialble and seeds collect on the ground.

description:
A Streaked Flycatcher (Myiodynastes maculatus), photographed at JardÃ­n BotÃ¡nico de Montevideo. [Local name: Benteveo Rayado.] The heavy white streaking on the brown upperparts, and the heavy brown streaking on the white underparts, actually seems to be distinctive, at least for the southern cone of South America.  One just has to study hundreds of pictures of birds in the relevant field guides to come to this conclusion!  Unfortunately, this bird did not stick around for long, so this is the only shot that I was able to take  of it.

This bird is a close relative of the Sulphur-bellied  Flycathcher (Myiodynastes luteiventris), a bird whose more northerly range takes it barely into Arizona.  That bird, however, has finer streaks on yellow underparts, a broader white malar patch, and a very bright, rufous tail.  (The tail of the Streaked Flycatcher in my photograph is indeed rufous, but not quite so bright.)  Sulphur-bellied Flycatchers do not normally range south of Costa Rica, so I think I am reasonably safe in calling my bird a Streaked Flycather.

Note: I have no prior experience with South American birds, so it is entirely possible that my identiciation is off.  I would welcome other suggestions as to what this bird could have been.

description:
An adult Southern Caracara (Caracara plancus), photographed at the JardÃ­n BotÃ¡nico de Montevideo, in Montevideo, Uruguay.  This bird is also known as the Southern Crested Caracara.  [Local names:  Carancho or Carancho ComÃºn.]

This was one of the first birds that I saw as I entered the park from Avenida de Dr. Luis Alberto de Herrera.  Its slow, lumbering flight with deep wingbeats reminded me of the flight style of a Northern Crested Caracara (Caracara jeriway, which I have seen in the American Southwest.  (The Northern Crested and Southern Caracaras are closely related, and at one point, they were even thought to be conspecific. )

I followed the caracara until it alighted in a huge tree, which is when I took this photograph.  The details from the photograph finalize the identification of this bird for me.   Its somewhat bulky, black shape overall; its large, yellow bill with orange to reddish cere; its black cap with a slight crest to the rear; its yellowish legs; and its large, white tail with brownish tip, are all consistent with Southern Caracara.

Note that I have no priori experience with the birds of South America, so it is entirely possible that my identification could be off.  I would welcome other suggestions as to what this bird might be.  This is my only photograph of this bird - it took off shortly after I had taken this shot.

description:
An adult and an immature Saffron FInch (Sicalis flaveola), photographed at Jardi­n Botanico de Montevideo, Uruguay. [Local name: Dorado.] The immature bird is located on the same branch as the adult, but 9 or 10 inches further down (towards the lower right-hand corner of the picture).  Note that, while these birds do bear some passing resemblance to the cardueline finches of North America, they are actually tanagers.

Although this part of South America does offer a broad array of bright, yellow, finch-like birds, apparently only the Saffron Finch and the Orange-fronted Yellow Finch (Sicalis colombiana) have adults with orange crowns and faces.  However, the latter bird is not found in Uruguay, never ranging south of the Cerrado biome in central Brazil, so it can be eliminated on the basis of range along.  This means that the birds in my phtograph are Saffron Finches.  

Here is a description of Saffron FInches from www.finchinfo.com that seems to fit the adult male bird quite well:

Physical descriptions
Black maxilla (upper beak), pale mandible (lower beak), greenish yellow back, yellow underparts, wing and tail feathers are black lined with yellow, dark pink legs. The male bird often has an orange forehead while the hen often has more dark streaks. 

All of these field marks are visible in the adult male bird in my photograph.  Females are supposed to be duller and streakier in general, while immature birds are all gray, with darker gray streaks and sometimes a few very limited and very subdued patches of yellow.

description:
A Southern Lapwing (Vanellus chilensis), foraging in the incoming tide along the Rio de La Plata in Montevideo, Uruguay.  [Local name: Tero ComÃºn.]  This is the national bird of Uruguay, and the only crested wader in South America.  When I was there, more or less at the peak of the Uruguayan summer, it was also virtually the only shorebird to be found along the Rio de la Plata.

The bird appears to be undergoing a molt, as its black crest appears to have molted out and begun growng back in, and the black on its face and breast seem much reduced from "normal."  Even so, it is still a quite distinctive bird, with its enormous, plover-like, reddish eyes; its downwardly slopiing, red-and-black bill; its dull, reddish-gray legs; and the smattering of bronze, coppery green, and black on its flight feathers.  This bird is about the size of a chicken, which surprised me, as for some reason, I had been expecting it to be more like a Killdeer in size.

The second shows the gull after it had flown a short distance, landing on another submerged rock.  There, it turned its head away from the camera more, giving one a good view of its auricular spot.

This was not one of the easiest birds to identify, and identification proceeded mainly by a process of elimination.  Identification was achieved as follows:

1) Clearly, this bird is in the Laridae, the broad family of birds that includes gulls and terns.  However, it does not have the "jizz" for a tern.  Terns have a more compact, streamlined structure to their bodies, often with short, thick necks and comparatively short legs that allows them to stand low to the ground.  When compared to the size of its body, the neck and legs of this bird are too long for it to be a tern.

2) Simple observation eliminates the oddities of the gull world from consideration.  It does not have the massive, bulky bill of a skimmer, nor does it have the killing machine looks of a jaeger, nor does it have the bulk and heft of  Skua. Consequently, skimmers, jaegers, and skuas can all be eliminated from consideration.

3) This leaves us with those gulls whose heads become white in adulthood (e.g, the so-called "white-headed gulls") vs. those gulls whose heads become some variation of black, brown, or gray in adulthood (e.g., the so-called "dark-headed gulls.").  Both sets of gulls go through a variety of plumage cycles before reaching maturity; what remains consistent, however, is the shape of the bill.  For white-headed gulls, the bill reminds me of a heavy-duty kitchen shears, with a tough upper mandible, sometimes hooked at the tip, and a heavy lower mandible, often with a prominent gonydeal angle.  The bill of even the smallest of the white-headed gullls is never as dainty or as delicate-looking as the bird in my photograph.  Therefore the bird in my photograph does not belong to the white-headed gull group.

4) In Uruguay, only two species of the dark-headed gull group are expected:  (1) the Grey-headed Gull (Chroicocephalus cirrocephalus) and (2) the Brown-hooded Gull (Chroicocephalus maculipennis).  Both species are year-round residents in the country.

5) The Grey-hooded Gull is a slightly larger bird than the Brown-hooded Gull, with a slightly bigger, slightly heavier, and noticeably longer bill.  Both birds will have dark irises when immature (and this bird is immature, as it has not developed a dark head yet), but the bill of an immature Grey-hooded Gull will be dull pink or pinkish orange with a black tip, while the bill of an immature Brown-hooded Gull will be dark red with a black tip.

6)  The immature Brown-hooded Gull will always have a dark auricular patch behind its eye.  The immature Grey-hooded Gull will also have this auricular patch behind the eye, but it can sometimes be connected to other grayish streaks or patterns on the crown or nape.  

7) Finally, the first and secondary primaries of the immature Brown-hooded Gull will retain a large white patch to it, which becomes quite visible when the bird is on the ground, with its wings folded.  The immature Grey-hooded Gull will also have white patch on its first and second primaries, but this white patch will not be as large, as pronounced, or as visible.  

Conclusion:  On the bases of the bill shape and color, as well as the white patches on the bird's frst and second primaries, this bird is an immature (first winter) Brown-hooded Gull.  Given that these photographs were taken in February, just past the middle of the austral summer and the peak of the austral breeding season, I think birds might even be recent fledgelings.

Caveat:  As I have no prior experience with South American birds, it is entirely possible that my identification of this bird is off.  This issue is compounded by the field guide that I have to work with, whose drawings of gulls and terns leave something to be desired.  Consequently, other suggestions as to what this bird might be are welcome.

Further caveat:  There is an actual Brown-headed Gull (Chroicocephalus brunneicephalus) the populates the Indian subcontinent, so care must be taked to call the bird in my photograph the Brown-hooded Gull (Larus maculipennis).  Otherwise, it gets very confusing!

description:
Three Neotropic Cormorants (Phalacrocorax brasilianus), photographed along the rocky shoreline of the Rio de la Plata in Montevideo, Uruguay.  I was already familiar with this species, having seen it in south Texas many years ago.  Here, near the other end of its natural range along the edge of the Rio de la Plata, they are called Váguas Comunes (after the local Indian name for cormorant, 'Vágua' or 'Bágua'.)

Neotropic Cormorants were virtually the only cormorant species that I saw along the Río de la Plata, from the Montevidean waterfront to Punta Carretas.  They're dowdier cousins to North America's Double-crested Cormorants, being both smaller in size and duller in color.  Their eyes are not quite the same piercing shade of green (in fact, they're more of a bluish-green), their bills and gular patches are not quite the same luminescent shade of orange, and their generally black plumage is not the same midnight hue of black,  muddied as it is by subtle undertones of brown and olive.  The white edge to its gular patch and its relatively long tail are both important field marks.

Also note that the bird on the far left has some brown on its throat, which appears to continue down to its belly.  This makes it a juvenile bird.  The two all-black birds on the right are both full adults.

tag_list: Chalk-browed Mockingbird, Mimus saturninus, Montevideo, Plazoleta Dr John Street, Rank 1, Uruguay
description:
A heavily feather-worn Chalk-browed Mockingbird (Mimus saturninus), photographed at the Plazoleta Dr. John Street in Montevideo, Uruguay. [Local name: Calandria ComÃºn.]  It is one of three Mimus species that can be found in Uruguay, the other species being the Patagonian Mockingbird (Mimus patagonicus) and the White-banded Mockingbird (Mimus triurus).  These other two species are seasonal, arriving in Uruguay during the austral fall and winter.  As this bird was photographed during the austral summer, it is unlikely that the bird in my photograph would be either of those species.  Even so, it would be good to compare them with the bird in my photograph and rule them out completely.

The White-banded Mockingbird (M. triurus) is the easiest of the two other birds to eliminate from consideration.  Although it has white supercilia (eyebrows), they are fairly subdued when compared to the eyebrows of the bird in my photograph.  It also has an eyeline that is barely noticeable, unlike the eyeline of the bird in my photograph.  What it does have are extensive bands of white across the wings, prominent white sides to its tail, and a rufous.  The White-banded Mockingbird is actually a far showier bird than the one in my photograph; its showiness just happens to be rear-loaded.

The Patagonian Mockingbird (M. patagonicus) has notable white supercilia, but they are not nearly as broad or as pronounced as the supercilia of the bird in my photograph.  It may also have adark eyeline, but that eyeline will also be not nearly as broad or pronounced at the bird in my photograph.  M. patagonicus does not have any streakiness to its back plumage, and its wing shape is also different; in M. patagonicus, the wings taper gradually, whereas the wings of the bird in my photograph narrow rapidly in the transition from the secondaries to the primaries.  This means that the wings of M. patagonicus tend to droop a bit, like those of an American Robin, whereas M. saturninus is able to hold its wings up against its tail.  Finally, the tail of the bird in my photograph exhibits at least one tail spot that has not faded or been erased by feather wear; however, the tail for M. patagonicus is completely black.  On the basis of all of these differences, I can eliminate M. patagonicus from further consideration.

Having eliminated all other possibilities, I must conclude that the bird in my photograph is the Chalk-browed Mockingbird, M. saturninus.

description:
A Rufous Hornero (Furnarius rufus), photographed Plaza IndependencÃ­a in Montevideo, Uruguay.  It took me a long time and quite a bit of searching through my field guide to figure out what this bird was.  In part, that was because this bird has no close relatives in North America.  It belongs to South America's Ovenbird Family (Funariidae), which are known for building mud nests that resemble old wood-burning ovens.  (South America's Ovenbirds are not related to North America's Ovenbird, Seiurus aurocapilla, which is an eastern wood warbler in the family Parulidae.)

Of the six species of hornero in South America, the Rufous Hornero is the only one that can be regularly found in Uruguay, where it has adapted well to human civiization. One can often find a pair of these birds lurking in any alleyway or cul-de-sac where even the smallest amounts of water and the tiniest bits of cover is available.  They seem to spend a lot of their time walking on the ground as they hunt for insects.  

This was the first decent shot of a Rufous Hornero that I was able to take when I was in Uruguay.  This bird seemed to be patrolling the grounds of the Artigas Mausoleum at the Plaza IndependencÃ­a, near downtown Montevideo.   It was almost as if it were serving as an honor guard for this national monument.

description:
A Great Grebe (Podiceps major), seen patroling the nearshore waters of the Rio de La Plata along the Rambla República Argentina in Montevideo, Uruguay.  This is a fairly distinctive bird amongst the grebes of southern South America.  Structurally, it reminds me of the Aechmophorus grebes of North America, with its long bill, long neck, and broad, buoyant body;  all of the other grebes in this part of South America are noticeably smaller and shorter-necked than this grebe, so I suppose it obtained its common and scientific names by default.  

Plumage-wise, the Great Grebe seems to find inspiration in the Northern Hemisphere's Red-necked Grebe (Podiceps grisegena).  The Great Grebe has a similar reddish-brown neck and dark gray body, but a face and bill that are both silvery gray. Its crest is also black, and gathered up in a bit of a pompadour, rather than being slicked back, as it would be for P. grisegena.  

The lead shot shows the grebe at its closest to the shoreline of the Rio de la Plata.  The subsequent shots show the bird as it moved away from the shoreline, eventually disappearing  amongst the river's choppy waves.

Three Whte-tufted Grebes (Rollandia rolland), photographed at high tide near the Parque de la Rambla in the Punta Carretas district of Montevideo, Uruguay.  These were small birds, no more than 12 inches (30 cm) long, with short necks and somewhat squarish heads.  They remind in some ways of the Northern Hemisphere's Horned Grebes (Podiceps auritus).

The bird towards the rear is an adult; note the heavy black shading to its crown, face, and nape, which allows the trademark white tufts around its eyes to stand out.  The two birds in the front are juveniles:  they have pale reddish-brown necks with just a hint of black down the rear; black foreheads and truncated crests containing a fair amount of grey; and white throats and faces, with one or two dark eyelines running past their auriculars.  Unfortunately, most of the field guides for the area don't show the juvenile plumages, so the juveniles can be confusing.

One last note:  this bird is also known as Rolland's Grebe.

description:
A Brown-hooded Gull (Chroicocephalus maculipennis) and a Snowy-crowned Tern (Sterna trudeau), perched on some rocks along the Rio de la Plata in Montevideo, Uruguay.  These birds were photographed from the Rambla República Argentina, between Dique Mauá and Playa Ramirez.  Both birds are in basic plumage, which is to be expected, as this photograph was taken towards the end of the Uruguayan summer.

The Brown-hooded Gull is the larger, taller bird standing furthest away from the camera.  Structurally, it is similar in size and shape to the Bonaparte's Gull of North America, which is one of its close relatives. It is a relatively small gull with a slight body and fairly short, dark reddish legs.  Its head is proportional to the rest of its body, with a fairly small, delicate, and slightly drooping reddish bill and a long, gradually rising forehead that ends in a small peak towards the rear of the bird's head.  Having already molted into basic plumage, this birdâs head and face are almost completely white, with just a small, dark auricular spot behind each eye.  This auricular spot is all that remains of the dark brown head and face that it sported during the summer months.

The Snowy-crowned Tern is the smaller, shorter bird closest to the camera.  It has the small, squat structure of an Arctic or Common Tern, with ridiculously small legs that seem as if they are about to collapse under the weight of the birdâs body.  Although a number of small terns frequent Uruguay's shoreline, this one can be identified by the odd, almost bulbous shape to its head; its long, slightly drooping bill; and the dark eyeline that recurves sharply behind each of its eyes.   In basic plumage (seen here), this bird's bill is black, with a bright yellow tip, and its legs are dark red to black.  In alternate plumage, its bill color becomes yellow, with a dark, vertical stripe near the tip, and its legs turn reddish.  I am a bit concerned about the underparts of this bird, which are supposed to be grayish in all plumages.  I do not seen any gray coloration on the tern's underparts in this picture; however, this could very well have been caused by feather wear and bleaching from the sun.

description:
A Gray-necked Wood-rail (Aramides cajanea), also known as a Gray-cowled Wood-Rail, photographed at El Jardí­n Botánico de Montevideo in Montevideo, Uruguay.  This bird was not only shy but quite a fast walker, so I had a hard time getting any photographs of it at all.  I was able to capture three somewhat fuzzy photos of it before it disappeared in some heavy brush; all of those photos are included here.

This was a large bird, about the size of a chicken and quite impressive.  Aside from Aramides cajanea, there is really only one other rail native to this area who would have this bird's large size, long legs, and large, heavy bill - the Giant Wood-rail, Aramides ypecaha.  However, the nape and the back of the neck in that species is reddish brown,  not grayish as is the case for the bird in my photos.   A. ypecaha also has a lighter, more pinkish breast than the bird in my photos, a bill that is slightly larger, and a slightly larger size overall.  For these reasons, A. ypecaha can be ruled out in favor of A. cajanea.

Note:  Locally, this bird is known as a Chiricote.

References:
1. De La Peña, Martí­n & Rumboll (1998).  Birds of Southern South America and Antarctica.  Princeton, NJ:  Princeton, University.  See Plate 29 for the species description of both A. cajanea and A. ypecaha.

description:
A Short-horned Grasshopper (Acrididae sp.), photographed on the tinted window of a business near the intersection of Bartolemé Mitre and Rincón in the Ciudad Vieja District of Montevideo, Uruguay.  This photograph was taken in the late spring, when Montevideo often experiences intrmittent showers and cool, gusty winds blowing in from the south or southwest. I discovered that, under these conditions, many of the local insects will take refuge on the walls and windows of the old buildings of Ciudad Viejo, below ample eaves that provide them with a bit of shelter.  Even so, this grasshopper was a bit of a surprise, as there isn't a lot of grass in Ciudad Vieja, especially where this grasshopper was photographed.  

Identifying this insect as a Short-horneed Grasshopper in the Acrididae family seems reasonable; note the relatively short antennae on this invididual.  However, as I know little about the grasshoppers of Uruguay, this is about as far as I can take the identification of his insect.  I certainly welcome any suggestions as to its genus and species identification.

Dimensions:  Body length was between 4 and 5 cm long.

description:
A Muscid Fly (Musca sp.), photographed at the Plaza Juan Pedro Fabini in the Centro District of Montevideo, Uruguay.  Note that there are two photographs in the set of pictures documenting this fly;  the first of these pictures provides an excellent view of the fly's antennae, while the second provides a better view of its wing venation.  The body of this fly was approximately 20mm in length and maybe 8mm at its broadest point.  The wings ar 10 to 11 mm long.

Identification of this insect as a Muscid-type fly was based on the following analysis:

1.  This insect has two wings, with what would have been the other pair of wings being reduced to a pair of position sensing mechanisms known as halteres.  (The halteres are unfortunately not visible in either photograph.)  This characeristic places this insect in the order Diptera, which encompasses a variety of two-winged, flying insects (flies).
2.  This fly has a pair of antenna projecting out from its forehead.  These antenna consist of three segments - an attachment point, a joint segment, and an enlarged and elongated paddle-like structure that has a small, hair-like appendage known as an arista.  In this case, the arista is plumose, meaning that the hair-like appendage has numerous side-bistles that give the appendage a feathery appearance.  This specific, three-segmented antenna structure places the fly in the sub-order Cyclorappha.  
3.  This fly has a wing with the following venation characteristics: (1) the vein closest to the body (vein A2 never reaches the wing margin, and (2) the next two veins that one encounters as one moves away from the body run parallel to each other.  Near the wing margin, the lower of these two veins bends sharply to connect to the other.  These wing veination characteristics indicate that this fly belongs to the genus Muscidae.
4.  Unfortunately, it is not possible to see the meron, an area of the the thorax just above the second pair of legs/, because it is heavily shaded.  The lack of bristles on the meron would further confirm that ths fly belongs to the genus Musca.
5.  This is as far as I can go with the identification of this fly.  Superficially, it seems to resemble the cosmopolitan Houe Fly (Musca domestica), especially with the four dark stripes on the uppermost surface of the thorax, the bristles on the thorax,and  the eyes being separate by a single, vertical stripe.  However, I do not know if there are any other, similar flies in Uruguay that might resemble the House Fly, or how I would distinguish them from the House Fly, so I will leave this insect identified to genus for now.

References:
1.  "How to Identify Flies" (n.d.), Zurqui All-Diptera Biodiversity Inventory.  Retrieved on 12/9/19 from http://phorid.net/zadbi/education/how-to-identify-flies/
2.  "Species Musca domestica - House Fly" (n.d.), Bug Guide.  Retrieved on 12/9/19 from https://bugguide.net/node/view/39559/bgpage
3.  "Family Muscidae - House Flies and Kin" (n.d.),  Bug Guide.  Retrieved on 12/9/19 from https://bugguide.net/node/view/7266
4.  "Morphology of Diptera" (n.d.), Wikipedia.  Retrieved on 12/9/19 from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphology_of_Diptera

tag_list: Foliolose Lichen, Lichen, Montevideo, Montevideo Department, Plaza España, Rank 1.5, Uruguay
description:
A Foliose Lichen (species unknown), photographed on the trunk of a palm tree at Plaza España in Montevideo, Uruguay.  Note that there are three photographs in the set of pictures documenting this lichen: 

(1) The lead shot, which provides a moderate closeup of the entire patch of lichen in situ.  Note the pale green thallus that becomes increasingly wrinkled and wart-like as one moves from the newest growth at the edge of the lichen patch to the oldest material at the center.  New growth at the edge of the thallus is charaterized by broad, round lobes that are up to 1 cm in radius.  Older growth is characterized by an extremely dense aggregation of soredia.   Overall dimensions of this lichen patch:  maximum of 4cm in the vertical direction and maximum of 3cm in the horizontal direction.

(2) The second shot, which provides a high magnification close-up of the soredia which dominate the central region of this patch of lichen.  

(3) The third and lost shot, which shows the underside of the lichen's thallus by lifting up one of its lobes.  Note that the underside of this lobe is uniformly dark brown in color, with a few rhizines to help attach this lichen to the wooden substrate below.

As I know virtually nothing about lichens in South America, I am going to leave the identification of this lichen to any experts within the iNaturalist community who might be interested in providing that identification.  That identification will, of course, need to take into consideration those characteristics described above.

tag_list: Eriopis connexa, Ladybird  Beetle, Ladybug, Montevideo, Montevideo Department, Plaza España, Rank 1, Uruguay
description:
I discovered this colorful ladybird beetle on the trunk of a palm tree at Plaza EspaÃ±a in the Ciudad Vieja District of Montevideo, Uruguay.  After some research on iNaturalist and elsewehere, I believe that this ladybird beetle belongs to the species Eriopis connexa (no common name, or at least none that I could find).  The elongated abdomen, slightly elongated pronotum, and comparatively large head (vis á vis other species of ladybird beetles) seem to be characteristic for the species.  The background color of both the abdomen and the pronotum is black.  Spot color for this species appears to be somewhat variable; however, in Uruguay, the spots are usually white, red, or some combination of the two colors.  There are six of these spots along the margin of the pronotum, and 14 spots distributed across the surface of the abdomen.  

Overall dimensions:  Eriopis connexa is a little bit bigger than a typical ladybug.  This one was about 8mm long and about 4mm wide

description:
Espécie livre que não ocorre no Brasil (ou então está mantida em cativeiro). Por esse motivo não posto no Wikiaves. 

Há cerca de 20 anos tenho fotografado tudo que tem vida. Acabei me especializando em pássaros e deixando outros organismos de lado. 

Não tinha um destino adequado às minhas fotos de outros organismos. Mas agora, através de amigos, descobri o *iNaturlist*. 

Estou me divertindo e organizando tudo na plataforma... Toda foto tem sua localização e data corretas (revisadas). Espero ajudar a comunidade com imagens úteis e também ser ajudado na ID dos organismos.

Na época que as fotos foram feitas, não tinha uma visão científica da coisa. Mas estou aprendendo e melhorando aos poucos. 

Não espero ter qualquer raridade catalogada, mas espero que possa ajudar em algo. Sou apenas um observador que gosta do assunto, não tenho capacitação técnica. 

Agradeço por toda a ajuda, identificações e correções. Já reencontrei e fiz muitos amigos nesta excelente plataforma.

Abração!!
@Manequinho

Se encontraron algunas especies creciendo en bosques nativos. Los árboles y la biología molecular podrían revelar que las especies brasileñas son nuevas para la 
ciencia." En el paper "What are the Laetiporus species present in southern South America?" los autores afirman que "basados en análisis filogenéticos sabemos que Laetiporus gilbertsonii es el nombre correcto para la especie que crece en sustratos nativos en el sur de América del Sur [Gleditsia y Schinus, por ejemplo] y la mayoría de los que crecen en Eucalyptus spp. La presencia de ejemplares filogenéticamente relacionados con Laetiporus sulphureus de Europa ha sido reportado en Uruguay creciendo sobre Eucalyptus spp.(Vasaitis et al., 2009), sin embargo no se han encontrado en nuestro muestreo". Hay que hacer más muestreos y análisis de los Laetiporus de América.
